title: BYU Head Coach Kalani Sitake on What Makes Jack Kelly Special | Giants Huddle | New York Giants
text: Welcome to another edition of the John Settle podcast brought to you by Citizens, the official bank of the Giants. I have John Schmilk coming to you from the Giants podcast studio presented by Hackin Sack, Meridian Health, Keep Getting Better. Fun show coming your way today. We're going to be joined by Kehlani Sitake. He's the head coach of BYU, coach Jack Kelly. There it will be the start of our coach series of coaches that coached the prospects that the Giants drafted in the 2026 NFL draft. And don't forget folks, go back uh our scouting series is up there as well on the Giants podcast which you can find on your favorite podcast platform, Giants YouTube channel, Giants.com/mpodcast, Giants app, it's all there. Check it out. We talked to the scouts that were in on the scouting process of the Giants first four picks in this year's draft. Arvar Ree, CC Mau, Noah, Colton Hood, and Malachi Field. So I really, really suggest you go check those out. a really good insight on the players and the Giant scouting process in terms of trying to find those guys. And now it's time to welcome in our guest for today. He is the head coach of BYU, Kehlani Sitake. Coach, thanks for being with us today, man. How are you? >> Great to be on. Thank you. >> All right, so let's talk about Jack Kelly. Uh he was a transfer to your program. What was it that when you watched him, you said, "I want this guy to be part of BYU." Well, I remember him in high school and it was one of those that that not highly recruited but but uh you you could see that he he was making plays on the on film and um and so when when it slipped through the cracks and he'd end up going to Weaver State, we kind of you kind of just see guys and all of a sudden he blew up and did some amazing things there. Um, and so when the portal happened, I I he went into the portal, we got him, and um, the last couple years he's been able to play for us has been amazing. And and he's he's way better than I even thought uh, from film in high school and even from Wever State. And so uh, having him here for the last two years has been amazing. Great leader for us. Um, doesn't say much, but does everything right. And then, uh, just really supportive as a teammate. It seems like everybody um gets better when they're around him and and he's he doesn't really care about the stats. I think he he's he can pass rush. That's one thing that he's really good at, but I think it it overshadows a lot of the stuff that he does uh well in in his zone drops and in his man-to-man coverage, how he plays the run. He he runs sideline to sideline. He can play any position. Um he's he's capable enough. He has a great football IQ and he can play any any of the linebacker positions where it's outside or inside. And then he's just he's just ferocious. he's a he's a he's a vicious player. And so it was always the battle was trying to make sure he doesn't get a targeting penalty and get kicked out of the game. And so that was always a worry for me. And um you know it's just like hey just hit him lightly and but what do you do when when you're trying to tell a guy to slow down and and it's hard but I can tell you one thing it's a lot easier for me as a head coach and for our our coaching staff to have to tell him to slow down than to speed up. So, he he will go all the way and he will do everything right and he loves the game and I think you guys are going to get a a great player. I think he's going to be a great partnership uh for the things that he can do. Um he's just a well-rounded player and then just a great person and a great teammate. >> Yeah, I want to dig into the on the field stuff, but first you mentioned the leadership part of this. He got to your program. I think he was basically named the captain right away, right? What does it say about a kid to come in from a small school, but then shows you enough as a player and as a guy to become a captain the first year he gets there? >> Well, I think it's all the little things that he does well off the field. Um, so I think it's a work ethic. He he didn't come in campaigning. He's not not a politician like that. Like he he he's quiet kid. He's softspoken, but he came in, worked hard, made a huge impact in the weight room, watched film, just try to get better. He just did all the little things, right? And and our team noticed um just the things that he does. Uh and so it's not like he was out there talking a lot. He probably probably doesn't talk very often, but but in the locker room, you can tell he he he's he gels with the players and then they they they just they kind of move towards him, which is really good. And I think I mean I think that I look at the roster and the guys that you have on the roster, there's a lot of people that I like. I mean like I like Jackson D. I've known him since he was since he was a a kid in high school, you know, and so I think he's going to gel really well with all the personalities with with Scataboo and all those guys. And so, um, this kid's a great young man. Um, I love coaching him. I'm sad that he's not here anymore, but, uh, I'm really excited for for I was kind of worried about where he would end up and after the Giants got him, I was really really excited that that he's going to be a Gman. >> Puddle up. Get in here. If you're lined up here, you got to go over the middle with it to score, >> right? How do we make that happen? >> I don't know, but Citizens does make sense of your money with Citizens. Official bank of Eli Manning. >> You mentioned a couple times now that he doesn't talk much, but he's a leader. So, is he a leader by example type of guy? Does he pull guys kind of off to the side privately and talk to them if he's not doing in front of the team? What's his leadership style? >> Yeah, he does all of that. I I think I mean he he can get up and stand in front of the team if he needs to, but he's not he's not going to be one of those guys that's going to going to try to do it that way. I think he'll do more of the private um discuss things with people and then it's just he's always trying to learn too. I mean, you talk about a defensive guy talking to offensive players, uh trying to learn what what they're doing. And then I I I'm always seeing him talk to offensive coaches. So, I mean, he has a connection with everybody. He's trying to learn more about the game. And then special teams, like we we tried to free him up and try to give him a little bit of rest on special teams and he was he was very offended, you know, like we took him off a punt and he took it like he took it personal. So I told the coaches just put him on whatever he wants and and uh you know, we just we're trying to free him up, let him play because we're asking him to do a lot uh especially this last season and he had to cover a lot of ground. We had him spy a lot of different athletic quarterbacks and and he did a great job with that. I mean, you look at what he was able to do uh his junior year in in in the Alamo Bowl against um Shadur and and and uh and Colorado and then just the stuff that he's been able to do. And then in the in the last game um you know, we we know we knew that we needed him to heal. He he he plays um he he he doesn't ever show that he's banged up, but he plays through everything. And then it I took it upon myself and our coaches on our staff to keep him safe. he he was going to play in that bowl game because you I mean we had to literally sit him down and say, "Hey, listen. You have a future in the NFL." And um he just But you know what's crazy? Once we did that, he he just changed and went right into coach mode. And um and and the guys that play that replaced him on the field made big plays because of him. And uh that's just where you're always going to get a guy that's going to be want to be in the facility. He's going to want to represent well, and he's going to give everything he has in for the team. and um that's hard to replace uh for us, but he left a huge impact in the young guys that are here and and for that I'm truly grateful. >> You mentioned his toughness a couple times already trying to play through injuries. He had a couple shoulder injuries, I know, in his final year there. And you think linebacker, shoulder injury, those are kind of important for what linebackers do, right? What did you see out of him that kind of showed that toughness that you will need to just, you know, survive everyday life in the National Football League? Well, I think those happened because we we put a lot on his plate. Uh especially his junior year, we we just probably overwhelmed him with too much. He played tons of special teams and played every snap on defense. And then we um I I think sometimes we we we take for granted the the young guys that can run and that are that are physical and then don't show any kind of um any kind of damage. And as we started working through it with sports with our sports science group, um we started realizing we're probably putting too much on his plate and that putting him at risk of injury. And so the the end of this last year, his senior year, was more of us taking care of him and and wanting to usher him into the NFL the right way. >> No, I think that makes sense. You talked about his intelligence. When he was a Weieber State coach, he was really more of an edge rusher, right? He was a guy that lined up on the edge and he tried to get after the quarterback and he still played linebacker, but he was more of an offball guy with you even though you did use him as as a pass rusher. How quickly was he able to adjust to that role, which is probably more the type of role he'll be asked to play here with the Giants off ball. >> Yeah, it was seamless transition. The guy was ready to do anything. He could play running back if you need him to. I mean, he's a he's a worldclass BMX writer, you know, so like those guys are crazy. And um so I mean he's just there's nothing you you you just put it right on him and you say, "Hey, we need you to do this. He can do it." I mean he's a great athlete. He could have played running back if we wanted him to. He could have he could have played tight end. I mean he he does things like block for punt return. I mean the guy just, you know, he and he and he goes hard all the time and and so I'm really really excited for him. Uh I think uh even though he doesn't say much, he'll make his he'll make a lot of noise on the field and then uh you guys don't have to worry about the targeting thing. It'll be worth sometimes for let allowing him to hit somebody and maybe get a penalty. It's it's it's okay for him to impose his will. That's he's an enforcer. I can't wait to see what he does for you guys. >> Yeah. So, you talked about him rushing the pass or being in force or hitting guys, but then you did mention his zone drops and I wonder is that one of the areas, coach, where you saw maybe him develop the most in your program because maybe he wasn't asked to do that quite as much where he came from. >> Yeah. And it was more of about his his if you're capable of getting you athletic enough to get your drops and he he can do all that stuff. Um he is so good at rushing the quarterback though and so I I know that that you know in the NFL a lot of guys can do that but it's nice to know that you can count on him if you're if you're bringing him in a blitz inside or outside. I mean he led our team in sacks and he and he didn't even blitz that much you know. So when you look at the ratio of his uh blitz to sack ratio it's really high. But if you look at the ratio of him being able to make an impact on the drops in his zones and even man-to-man coverage, he he does a great job at all that. So, um, the kid's a great young man and and I'm really fired up. I I just sky's the limit for him. I mean, I I I coached Fred Warner and Fred Warner didn't play a lot of inside backer. He played mostly um off the ball. We put him even in nickel. We put him in in a rover position a lot like we did with Jack. And and then he goes to the NFL and plays middle linebacker. And I think uh it's nice to be right about that one, too. So, I I feel just as confident about Jack. >> If you want to know how to manage 2 minutes of crunchtime football, I'm your man. But if you're wondering about a long-term financial plan, you should talk to Citizens. Hey, I can also talk lawn care. I'd like to learn about a mowing routine. >> Yes, I knew I could help. >> Make sense of your money with Citizens. From game day celebrations to your everyday financial needs, Big Blue fans get the most out of every moment with Citizens. Learn more at citizensbank.com/giants. It is funny. You talk about moving from the edge to offball with you guys. You know, there's a lot of instinctual things, right? Being able to see it and understanding where the run's going, your responsibilities are different. Did his instincts just take over? Is that why you think it was so natural for him able to kind of transition to that off the ball spot from where he was on the line of scrimmage? >> Of course. And I think the the the goal is probably not to over coach him and just I think you know you you want to it's kind of weird. It's like it's like if you're teaching basketball and you're teaching the concept of shooting a layup like you dribble the ball and then there's these these steps that you go through and you you know you take the two steps you throw the ball into the corner of of the box and it and it goes in and then and then you probably never shoot a layup like that for the rest of your career unless you want to get it squatted, you know. So >> yeah. So in football, you teach the basics on on your stance and where you got to be and then you just kind of let them go and and and um I think uh we've we we try to control too much and I think the the the main thing is teach the principle. Let this guy do it and he will surprise you and what he can do. >> No, I think that makes sense. You said you were concerned where he might go, but you were happy he wound up in New York. Why did you think this is going to be such a good fit for him? >> Well, I know I know the personnel there. I know the coaches. I I know the the brand and I and I and I know what's the expectations are. I I know the fans and what they're what they want and they're going to get it from him. I mean, the the uh I I know maybe they don't know enough about him, but if you go watch the film and you go see his personality and you see what he's all about, he's a perfect fit for New York. And he's and he's going to be it's going to be a a great um a great partnership. And I think more than anything like he's going to give everything he has and that's what that's what you and the fans want there and the high expectations of tradition and and he'll come in here and he'll make a splash but he won't he's not a highmaintenance kid man he's he he'll work hard and uh you know you're going to get your return on investment definitely for sure. >> Now he's going to have some help from Jackson with this going from Utah to the big city of New York City right? So, how do you think he's going to make that jump, you know, coming here, which is a much different environment than maybe what he had out there in Utah? >> Uh, you don't have to worry about him. He'll be fine. I think I think uh Jackson was will take him around and show him some of the sites, but this guy only thing he wants to see is the facility, football field, and the film room, and that's probably what you're going to see him doing mostly. >> I love it. Coach, anything else that that anecdotes, stories, interactions with him that that you think would kind of give fans an idea of exactly what Jack's all about and what he's going to bring not only to the football field, but also to the community. >> I think for me is like I'm I'm not I made a lot of statements already about what I what I think he's going to do. Uh and and people can say whatever they want about it. I I think he probably didn't want me talking about him too much. He if he knew I was talking like this, he'd probably be like, "Coach, that's enough." because the truth is I think he just wants to prove it and and so I I'm to to respect him. I I've said a lot and I probably put a lot of expectations on him, but no more than he's put on himself, but I think he's not a talk first guy. He's he's going to walk the walk and you guys will see for yourself. >> Coach, this was great. I really appreciate all the information on Jack. I can't wait to see him on the field.
